planting.note: Direct sow shortly before the last frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop; Snow White was collected as a traditional cool-season green near Nanjing, China, and its stems sweeten noticeably after exposure to light frost.

directions: Direct sow thinly in fertile, moisture-retentive soil, thinning seedlings once true leaves appear; Snow White is a tall heirloom bok choy type distinguished by unusually broad, glistening white petioles topped with crisp, dark green leaves. Unlike many bok choy types that need full sun to size up quickly, Snow White holds its quality and resists premature bolting when given afternoon shade during the warmer edges of the growing season, making it a useful pick for beds that only get partial light. Harvest whole heads once the thick white stems have filled out, or take outer stalks individually for a longer cut-and-come-again season; the crunchy stems are good raw, and both stems and leaves hold up well in stir-fries and soups.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost, and again from late summer into fall; Suzhou Baby is a market-garden staple around Suzhou, China, valued for holding tender texture even as heads size up and for tolerating only a few hours of direct sun per day.

directions: Direct sow into fertile, evenly moist soil and thin to allow heads room to fill out into their characteristic tight, rounded form. Suzhou Baby forms a dense, compact rosette of pale green petioles and rounded, glossy leaves that stays tender and mild-flavored well past the size where many baby bok choy types turn fibrous, and it shrugs off both a warm spell and a light cold snap better than most spring-planted greens. Because it needs only a partial day of direct sun to size up properly, it performs well tucked into beds that get shade from taller neighboring crops for part of the day. Harvest whole heads at the base once they feel firm, or pick outer leaves progressively for a steady kitchen supply.

planting.note: Direct sow every 3-4 weeks from before the last frost into fall for a continuous supply; Hedou traces to a village near Hong Kong and forms mature heads no bigger than a large grape, so tight successive sowings keep the harvest coming.

directions: Direct sow shallowly and keep the soil surface consistently moist, since this micro bok choy's shallow roots dry out quickly compared to standard-sized types. Hedou produces miniature, whole heads barely larger than a bite, with pale stems and small tender leaves that need no chopping before cooking, and it thrives in the light shade of a container on a partly shaded porch or the dappled edge of a garden bed. Its small stature and fast pace make it forgiving of less-than-full sun, since a shorter daily light window still lets it reach harvest size before bolting becomes a concern. Pick whole heads at the base as soon as they firm up, and resow every few weeks for uninterrupted harvests through the cool season.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost and again in late summer for fall harvest, sowing in succession every couple of weeks; Baby Milk matures quickly to single-serving size and is best harvested promptly before hot weather or a hard freeze sets in.

directions: Direct sow thickly and thin gradually, using early thinnings as baby greens while remaining plants size up into small, palm-sized heads. Baby Milk forms neat, compact rosettes of ivory-white stems and dark green leaves that mature quickly enough to fit into tight rotations between other crops, and its small footprint and tolerance of a partly shaded spot make it well suited to container culture on a porch or balcony. Because heads reach usable size in about a month, it is an efficient way to work fresh bok choy into partially shaded beds that would leave slower crops undersized. Harvest whole heads at the base as soon as they feel firm, since older plants lose their tender, single-serving texture.

planting.note: Direct sow before the last frost, and again in late summer for a fall and winter crop; Old Tokyo is a traditional Tokyo-area strain of komatsuna that has been grown as a cool-season spinach substitute for generations.

directions: Direct sow into fertile soil and thin progressively, eating the thinnings as baby greens while remaining plants develop into full-sized rosettes. Old Tokyo carries the smooth, glossy, dark green leaves and mild, faintly sweet, spinach-like flavor typical of heirloom komatsuna, with a slightly milder bite than many modern hybrid strains. It grows well in the dappled light under taller crops or along the partly shaded edge of a bed, needing less direct sun than full-sized napa cabbage or mustard greens to size up properly. Harvest outer leaves continuously from about a month after sowing, or cut whole rosettes at the base once they reach full size; cold weather sweetens the flavor further.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners
